procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 25.04.2007 of the High Court of Judicature at Madras in Criminal Appeal No. 804 of 2006.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant, Murugan, filed an appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 804 of 2006) in the High Court of Judicature at Madras challenging his conviction and sentence awarded by the Additional Sessions Judge. The High Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the judgment of the Additional Sessions Judge.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Murugan, feeling aggrieved by the High Court's decision, approached the Supreme Court by way of a special leave petition, which was converted into Criminal Appeal No. 1498 of 2010. The Supreme Court heard the appeal and ultimately dismissed it, finding no merit.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in its appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, should interfere with the concurrent findings of fact recorded by the lower courts against the accused.

facts: The appellant was convicted by the Additional Sessions Judge for offences under Sections 364 and 302 of the IPC.
The High Court upheld the conviction on appeal.
The appellant then appealed to the Supreme Court, challenging these concurrent findings of fact from the two lower courts.
law: The Supreme Court has a settled legal principle that under its appellate jurisdiction (Article 136), it will be slow to interfere with concurrent findings of fact recorded by lower courts.

The Court will not re-appreciate the evidence 'de novo' (from the beginning) unless it is shown that the lower courts either failed to consider relevant evidence or that their findings are perverse or absurd.
application: Despite the general rule of non-interference, the Supreme Court made an "endeavour to peruse the evidence" to determine if the lower courts' findings were legally and factually sustainable.
After reviewing the evidence, the Court concluded that the findings were indeed sustainable and that the two lower courts were right to hold the appellant guilty.
The Court found that the conviction was correctly based on a proper appreciation of the ocular (eyewitness) and circumstantial evidence presented by the prosecution.
The Court determined that none of the exceptions to the rule of non-interference applied, as there was no perversity, absurdity, or failure to consider evidence in the lower courts' decisions.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided not to interfere with the concurrent findings of the lower courts. It held that there was no good ground to take a different view because the conviction was based on a proper appreciation of evidence and the findings were legally and factually sustainable, thus rejecting the appeal on this issue.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in its appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, should interfere with the concurrent findings of fact recorded by the lower courts against the accused.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the concurrent findings of the two lower courts, which held him guilty, were flawed and not legally or factually sustainable, thus requiring the Supreme Court to interfere and reverse the conviction.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the concurrent findings of the lower courts were based on a proper appreciation of evidence, were legally and factually sustainable, and therefore, there was no merit in the appeal that would warrant interference from the Supreme Court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When lower courts have recorded concurrent findings against an accused person based on due appreciation of evidence, the Supreme Court, under Article 136 of the Constitution, will be slow to interfere with such findings and will not re-evaluate the evidence unless it is shown that the lower courts failed to consider relevant evidence or that their findings are perverse or absurd.
obiter: The two Courts below were right in holding the appellant guilty of commission of the offences by properly appreciating the ocular evidence of the prosecution witness notwithstanding the death of the main accused, which was of no relevance for deciding the involvement of the appellant in commission of crime.
The two courts below rightly held that the appellant’s conviction was based on circumstantial evidence which, in this case, the prosecution was able to prove it by adducing evidence.
The prosecution was able to prove the chain of circumstances/events appearing against the appellant without any break therein and hence, the appellant’s conviction deserves to be upheld.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court will not interfere with concurrent findings of fact recorded by lower courts, which are based on a due appreciation of evidence, unless it is shown that the lower courts failed to consider relevant evidence or that their findings are perverse or absurd. In this case, after reviewing the evidence, the Court found that the concurrent findings holding the appellant guilty were legally and factually sustainable, based on a proper appreciation of the evidence, and therefore, there was no good ground to take a different view.
legal_tests_applied: When the Courts below have recorded concurrent findings against the accused person which are based on due appreciation of evidence, this Court under Article 136 of the Constitution of India would be slow to interfere in such concurrent findings and would not appreciate the evidence de novo unless it is prima facie shown that both the Courts below did not either consider the relevant piece of evidence or there exists any perversity or/and absurdity in the findings recorded by both the Courts below.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant failed to demonstrate any infirmity, perversity, or absurdity in the concurrent findings of the lower courts that would justify the Supreme Court's interference.
Upon its own review of the evidence, the Supreme Court concluded that the findings of the two lower courts were legally and factually sustainable in law.
why_respondent_won: The concurrent findings of the lower courts were based on a proper appreciation of the evidence, specifically the ocular evidence of the prosecution witness.
The Supreme Court, after its own examination, concurred with the reasoning and conclusion of the lower courts, finding no good ground to take a different view.
policy_considerations: The Supreme Court, in its appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, should be slow to interfere with concurrent findings of fact and should not appreciate the evidence de novo, preserving its role for cases where there is a clear error like perversity, absurdity, or non-consideration of vital evidence by the lower courts.
